::: {.topic-banner}
**The purpose**

Use R to make your analytical reasoning visible. The goal is not to memorise every function; it is to understand the data flowing through the analysis and connect every output to a clinical question.
:::

## The REBM R workflow

::: {.code-flow}
<div><span>1</span><strong>Question</strong><small>Define population, exposure, comparator, outcome and time.</small></div>
<div><span>2</span><strong>Import</strong><small>Load packages and read unchanged source data.</small></div>
<div><span>3</span><strong>Prepare</strong><small>Select, filter, recode and document missingness.</small></div>
<div><span>4</span><strong>Describe</strong><small>Inspect counts, distributions and plausible values.</small></div>
<div><span>5</span><strong>Analyse</strong><small>Estimate, visualise and check assumptions.</small></div>
<div><span>6</span><strong>Interpret</strong><small>Translate magnitude, uncertainty and limitations.</small></div>
<div><span>7</span><strong>Preserve</strong><small>Store decisions, results, versions and exports.</small></div>
:::

## Four rules that prevent most problems

1. **Never modify the only copy of the source data.** Create a clearly named analysis object.
2. **Inspect the result of every important transformation.** Code running without an error does not prove it did what you intended.
3. **Save analytical results as objects.** Do not repeatedly copy numbers by hand.
4. **Keep interpretation beside output.** A table or model object without clinical meaning is unfinished.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Make any page printable

Use your browser’s **Print → Save as PDF** option. Toolkit pages include print-friendly styling so they can become personal one-page or multi-page references.
